name: Shape measured from the font files (outline statistics: weight, width, slant, x-height, stem, stroke contrast, squareness)
what_it_is: A handful of numbers per font face, computed from the glyph outlines of a-z, H, x, l and o with fontkit (the reader the app already uses in src/facts/). What I measured: weight = summed ink area of a-z divided by summed advance width, divided by the em (the fontTools measureWeight idea); width = mean advance (measureWidth) and advance over x-height; slant = area-weighted covariance(x,y) / variance(y) of the glyph shapes, as an angle (the fontTools StatisticsPen / measureSlant definition); x-height ratio (x over H); stem thickness of l at mid-height; stroke contrast of o (side strokes against top and bottom strokes); squareness of o (outer contour area over its bounding box: a circle is 0.785, a rounded square is 0.9 or more); straight-segment share (length of line segments over total outline length of a-z). For comparison I also read the cheap table values in the files (OS/2 usWeightClass and usWidthClass, post.italicAngle, PANOSE), which turned out to be mostly defaults. Output is about 10 numbers per face, roughly 150 KB for the whole catalog.
provider_and_url: No outside provider: we compute it. Definitions follow fontTools (varLib.avar.plan measureWeight / measureWidth / measureSlant, which use fontTools.pens.statisticsPen.StatisticsPen): https://github.com/fonttools/fonttools/blob/main/Lib/fontTools/varLib/avar/plan.py and https://fonttools.readthedocs.io/en/latest/pens/statisticsPen.html . Prior art measuring the same things: FontBase SuperSearch (x-height, weight, contrast, proportion, measured automatically for any font added; https://fontba.se/blog/super-search ), Adobe Fonts filters (weight, width, x-height, contrast, case, figures; FontBase says Adobe classifies in-house, which I could not verify), Florian Schulz, The Anatomy of a Thousand Typefaces (opentype.js on Google Fonts; https://medium.com/@getflourish/the-anatomy-of-a-thousand-typefaces-f7b9088eed1 ), tfrere/fontmap (fontTools proportions blended into a CLIP map; https://github.com/tfrere/fontmap ). In the app: fontkit, see src/facts/core.ts.
catalog_coverage: Counted by me (node SCRATCH/vv/measure.mjs, results in SCRATCH/vv/m-google.jsonl, m-indie.jsonl, m-italic.jsonl; SCRATCH is the session scratchpad from the brief). 2,082 of 2,099 families measured (99.2%): Google 1,743 of 1,760; Fontshare 64 of 64; Velvetyne 63 of 63; Collletttivo 26 of 26; Tunera 23 of 23; Use & Modify 163 of 163. The 17 Google failures: 10 colour or layered fonts whose glyphs have no plain outline in the file (Bitcount Grid Double Ink, Bitcount Grid Single Ink, Bitcount Ink, Bitcount Prop Double Ink, Bitcount Prop Single Ink, Bitcount Single Ink, Foldit, Honk, Kalnia Glaze, Sixtyfour Convergence); 5 whose CDN subset lacks the H or x glyph I measure from (Bungee Tint, Cairo Play, Coral Pixels, OpenDyslexic, Reem Kufi Fun); and 2 file problems (Open Sauce Sans: unknown format from the CDN; Chiron Sung HK: 404 for its latin-400 file). Of the 2,082, all nine outline measures exist for 2,069; 13 have no lowercase set to measure, and stroke contrast is missing for 115 (pixel and similar fonts whose o has no clean side and top strokes). Italic faces: 478 of the 479 italic families measured in a second pass. For checking against Google's human tags: 1,613 of the 1,760 Google families have tags (1,598 of them measured); none of the 339 non-Google rows has any.
granularity: Per face: one upright face per family (the file nearest weight 400) and one italic face where the catalog lists one. Variable-font axes and other weights are not measured; fontkit can instantiate variable fonts, so a second pass at wght 100 and 900 is possible, but I did not run it. Google's own quant.csv has per-instance stroke widths but covers only 1,399 of the 1,760 catalog Google families.
signal_type: Geometric shape: weight, width, slant, x-height, stroke contrast, squareness. No semantic mood. Mood has to be inferred from the shape, either by the LLM reading the numbers or by a regression onto Google's tags (works partly, see below).
mood_dimensions_covered: All numbers are mine (python3 SCRATCH/vv/analyze.py, analyze2.py, analyze4.py, analyze6.py) on the 1,598 Google families that have both a Google tag row and a measurement. Tag weights are Google's family-level rows (the rows with an empty instance column in families.csv). That file also holds per-instance rows such as wght@900, which I excluded because I measure the regular face; a missing tag counts as 0. Spearman unless stated. 'AUC' is a held-out 5-fold ridge model on 15 traits, tag weight >= 50 against the rest, with folds grouped by the first word of the family name so Noto Sans * or Bitcount * are held out together; 'category-only' is the same model fed only Google's category, which is what the prompt already carries. MOTION / ACTIVE: the claim replicates. Google's legacy 1-10 slant against Active: Pearson 0.51 (n=712, the only families that have legacy values; Spearman 0.42). My measured slant (absolute degrees) against Active: rho 0.35, available for every family. Held-out AUC for Active >= 50 is 0.91 from traits (category-only 0.79). The strong cue is an upright face drawn slanted: of 158 faces with measured slant >= 8 degrees, 38% are Active >= 50 against a 5.8% base rate (122 of the 158 are handwriting, 30 display, 5 sans; the 36 non-handwriting ones reach 42% against 2.8%). 'Has a real italic' is the opposite cue: 1% Active (n=330). Active also leans on curved outlines (straight-segment share rho -0.32, squareness -0.24) and low contrast (-0.18). Excited behaves the same (straightness -0.43, slant 0.38, AUC 0.84). Slant alone is not 'fast': the top 25 faces by slant are mostly formal copperplate scripts (Monsieur La Doulaise, Pinyon Script, Mr De Haviland, Italianno) and only 8 of those 25 carry Google's Active tag; precision at 50 is 40% (about 7 times the base rate) but the list needs a category or weight filter. LOUD: the claim replicates. Legacy thickness against Loud: Pearson 0.77 (n=714; Spearman 0.73). Measured weight against Loud: rho 0.72; stem thickness 0.63; usWeightClass 0.02 (it is 400 for nearly everything). Held-out AUC 0.96 (category-only 0.75). FUTURISTIC / TECHNO: 'nothing tracks it' holds for Google's legacy values (|r| <= 0.11 for thickness, slant and width against both tags) but not for outline shape: squareness of o against Futuristic rho 0.38 and straight-segment share 0.36 (Techno 0.19 and 0.24), x-height ratio 0.21. Held-out AUC 0.88 for Futuristic (category-only 0.69) and 0.88 for Techno (0.70), but rho only 0.41 and 0.29. A hand rule (squareness + straightness + 0.5 width) puts 34% Futuristic in its top 50 (base 5.3%) and 40% Techno (base 6.2%); its top 25 is pixel, barcode and blocky display faces (Press Start 2P, Geostar, Stalinist One, Libre Barcode 39, Orbitron), so it finds 'squared', not the whole mood. CALM: weak (AUC 0.84 against 0.83 category-only); mostly 'not slanted, not heavy'. ELEGANT / SOPHISTICATED: rho with slant 0.35, narrow width -0.31, low x-height -0.31 (48 positives, ungrouped AUC 0.97, small n). HANDMADE: straightness -0.42, slant 0.36, squareness -0.37 (Handwritten AUC 0.92), but Google's category already says handwriting. PLAYFUL / HAPPY: round outlines (Playful straightness -0.47; AUC 0.80 and 0.85). NOT CAPTURED: Sincere (AUC 0.67, below category-only 0.70), Innovative (0.74), Rugged (0.74), Art Deco (0.73, only 9 positives).
query_style_specificity: Helps most for tight, shape-bound requests (heavy, thin, condensed, wide, squared, slanted, round, high contrast), where a number answers the request directly. Weaker for loose affective words: Sincere AUC 0.67 (below category-only), Innovative 0.74, Calm 0.84 against 0.83 for category alone. For 'fast movement or action' it helps (slant on an upright face plus curved outlines) but only with a script and display filter, because slant alone returns wedding scripts.
quality_evidence: Replication of the claimed evidence, on 1,598 families with family-level Google tags: legacy slant against Active r=0.51 (claimed 0.51: confirmed); legacy thickness against Loud r=0.77 (claimed 0.77: confirmed, n=714); nothing legacy tracks Futuristic or Techno (|r| <= 0.11: confirmed), but outline squareness and straightness do (rho 0.38 and 0.36 for Futuristic). Trap I fell into and other items may too: families.csv holds Google's tags per instance (a second column such as wght@900, 1,939 families have a default row, many variable families also have rows at other weights). A first pass that kept the last row per family gave thickness against Loud only 0.60 because it mixed in the Black instance; with the family-level rows it is 0.77. Held-out prediction (grouped 5-fold, AUC for tag >= 50, traits against category-only): Active 0.91 / 0.79, Excited 0.84 / 0.78, Loud 0.96 / 0.75, Futuristic 0.88 / 0.69, Techno 0.88 / 0.70, Stiff 0.92 / 0.62, Playful 0.80 / 0.75, Happy 0.85 / 0.74, Calm 0.84 / 0.83; ungrouped Sincere 0.67 / 0.70. Ungrouped 5-fold gave the same values within 0.03 (the Sincere figure comes from the ungrouped run). Same 48 fonts rated blind by vision models (see the vision-labels item; stratified sample, so AUCs are optimistic and n is small): traits AUC Active 0.94, Futuristic 0.81, Loud 0.99, Calm 0.89 against a Sonnet-class model reading images 0.89, 0.89, 0.98, 0.80; the two combined (rank sum) 0.97, 0.91, 1.00, 0.91. Literature: I found no published test of measured-trait search against mood words. The closest: the FontCLIP paper's Table 2a reports hand-made vector features at 65.73% pairwise attribute accuracy (chance 50%) against 65.32% for FontCLIP, i.e. geometry is as good as the best fine-tuned CLIP on O'Donovan's attributes (https://anranqi.github.io/img/fontCLIP.pdf). I did not run any of this through the real LLM search.
known_noise: Unmeasurable: 17 families (0.8%); 13 more lack lowercase measures; contrast missing for 115. Estimator limits: the covariance slant underestimates strongly cursive faces; against post.italicAngle on the 431 italic faces that have a table angle it correlates only 0.43 (medians 10.0 and 9.4 degrees). It is measured at the weight nearest 400 only, so a family's bold or condensed cuts are invisible. The file tables are the noisy part, which is the reason to measure: post.italicAngle is 0 for 168 of the 176 upright faces that measure >= 8 degrees of slant (the italic bit is set on only 4 of them) and for 47 of the 478 real italic faces; usWeightClass says 400 for about 2,000 faces whose measured weight spans 0.147 to 0.335 em (10th to 90th percentile; for Google this is partly by construction because I took the 400 file); usWidthClass is the default 5 for 98% of Google, 100% of Fontshare, 94% of Velvetyne, 65% of Collletttivo, 100% of Tunera and 89% of Use & Modify faces; PANOSE weight or contrast is non-zero in only 38% of Google, 2% of Fontshare, 51% of Velvetyne, 0% of Collletttivo, 17% of Tunera and 67% of Use & Modify faces.
name_and_memory_bias: None from names: the numbers come from outlines only, so evocative names (Orbitron, Bungee, Hurricane) cannot leak in and an indie font is treated like Roboto. Two softer biases remain: the LLM that reads the numbers translates request words into traits from its own memory, and the Google tags I validated against were made by people looking at the fonts, so they share some taste with the shape.
untagged_rows: Ranked fairly: all 339 non-Google rows and the 137 Google families without tags get the same numbers as everyone else. Only the 17 unmeasured families would drop out silently; give them a neutral fallback (category) or measure them in a browser canvas. Indie and Fontshare faces sit inside Google's range on most traits (median weight 0.202 em against 0.209, straight share 0.52 against 0.50, squareness 0.80 against 0.80) except stroke contrast (median 0.08 against 0.19), so a mapping learned on Google should transfer, but that is untested because indie fonts have no Google tags [uncertain]. A name-only check I did not judge visually: ranking indie and Fontshare faces by the traits-to-tag regression puts Kihim, Sharpie, Louise, Interlope and Britney first for Active, and 0xA000 Pixelated, Ferrite Core DX, FT88 and jgs first for Techno and Futuristic.
text_interference_risk: Not applicable: nothing is rendered or read as text; the numbers come from outlines.
integration_path: Data file: server/data/traits.json, written by a new builder script next to the others (fontkit and the indie file cache are already there): {family: {w: 0.209, wd: 0.50, xr: 0.72, sl: 1.2, st: 0.17, ct: 0.19, sq: 0.80, sf: 0.50, it: 0, isl: 9.4}} for 2,082 families, about 150 KB. My run: 81 s wall for the 1,743 Google faces (27 s CPU), about 33 s for indie and Fontshare, 34 s for italics. Route 1 (cheapest, no extra call): turn the numbers into plain words only where a trait is extreme and append them to the catalog row in compactCatalog, e.g. 'Teko | sans | fontsource | semibold, condensed, squared'. Cut-offs I tried: weight at the catalog's 10th, 30th, 70th and 90th percentile (thin, light, semibold, bold); advance over x-height at the 15th and 85th (condensed, wide); upright slant >= 6 degrees (slanted); squareness >= 0.86 or straight share >= 0.62 (squared), straight share <= 0.2 (round); contrast >= 0.55 (high-contrast). Result: 480 rows get no word, 542 get one, 594 two, 397 three, 84 four, 2 five. Route 2 (needs a scoring step): the LLM first turns the request into trait wishes (slant: oblique, outlines: curved, weight: heavy, exclude: script), plain code ranks all 2,082 rows with the numbers (under 1 ms), and the LLM re-ranks a shortlist. This is where 'fast' gets its filter: slant plus curved outlines plus a category that is not script. Route 3: feed the same numbers into the tag-transfer item, predicting Google tag weights for untagged rows (the ridge on 15 traits behind the AUCs above).
tokens_per_row: Words route: 29,921 added characters over 2,099 rows = 14 characters, about 3.6 tokens per row, about 7.5k tokens in total, roughly +19% on the current catalog text (159,799 characters, about 40k tokens). Both are characters/4 estimates, not tokenizer counts [uncertain]. Stays cacheable: the numbers are static, so the catalog block of the system prompt only changes when the catalog or the cut-offs change.
vocabulary_alignment: Adds plain design words (thin, bold, condensed, wide, slanted, squared, round, high-contrast), not Google's mood tags. They map onto Google's vocabulary only through the regression (traits to Active, Loud, Futuristic and so on, held-out AUC 0.84 to 0.96 for most moods in the table above), so a second route is to emit predicted Google tags for untagged rows.
explainability: Strong: 'slanted 28 degrees, curved outlines' or 'weight 0.34 em' is a measured value a person can check by eye.
determinism: Deterministic: the same files give the same numbers. The search result stays as variable as today's LLM call unless a plain-code scoring step is added.
build_effort: Small to medium, about 1 agent-day: port SCRATCH/vv/measure.mjs (about 200 lines, already works on all 2,082 faces) into a server script following src/facts/core.ts conventions, add a unit test pinning a few known fonts (an upright sans, an italic, a monospace), choose cut-offs, change compactCatalog, and rerun server/check-vibe.ts on 20-30 queries. The Python route needs fonttools, which was not installed here (python3 had no fontTools); the Node port avoids a new dependency.
per_search_cost_and_latency: Nothing added per search with the words route beyond about 7.5k more cached prompt tokens; I did not time the change (the app's own comment measures a follow-up at about 7 s with thinking off) [uncertain]. A scoring step before the LLM adds either one short extra call or folds into the same call; ranking 2,082 rows in plain code is under 1 ms.
one_off_cost: No dollars. Google: 1,743 woff2 files (93 MB) read from jsDelivr into memory and not saved; 478 italic faces 22 MB; Fontshare 64 files plus the 275 cached indie files 15.9 MB together. About 2.5 minutes wall in total here, 4 requests in parallel with 120 ms spacing.
human_effort: About 1 hour to look at rendered rows near each cut-off and set them, and 1 hour to rate a grid for 20 queries. None as the catalog grows (rerun the script).
asset_access: Open and politely fetchable. Google: Fontsource latin woff2 on cdn.jsdelivr.net (fontsource/fonts/<id>@latest/<subset>-<weight>-normal.woff2), 1,743 of 1,760 read; the subset keeps the OS/2 and post tables. Fontshare: cdn.fontshare.com, 64 of 64 fetched (the app already proxies it). Indie: all 275 files were already in server/.cache/fonts (named by the sha1 of the URL, no extension): Velvetyne 63 (from GitLab), Collletttivo 26, Tunera 23, Use & Modify 163. Nothing was requested from velvetyne.fr.
licence_and_provenance: Numbers measured from outlines are facts about a shape, not a copy of the font. Catalog licences (counted from cat.json): Google rows OFL 1,716, Apache 36, UFL 5, other 3; indie mostly OFL (Velvetyne 62 plus 1 Bitstream Vera, Collletttivo 26, Tunera 23, Use & Modify 132 OFL plus CC BY 10, GPL with font exception 4, Bitstream Vera 5 and a few others); Fontshare 63 rows under the ITF Free Font License (free for personal and commercial use, no redistribution or resale of font files); I found no ITF wording about measuring fonts or AI use [uncertain]. Storing measurements does not redistribute a font. Validation data: Google's families.csv tags (the brief calls the same tags CC BY 4.0 through the API; I did not verify the licence of the CSV copy).
etiquette: Fontsource files via jsDelivr at 4 requests in parallel with 120 ms spacing (1,743 + 478 requests); Fontshare CDN at 2 in parallel with 700 ms spacing (64 requests); a handful of single requests to GitHub raw and the GitHub API. No robots-blocked or bot-protected sites. velvetyne.fr never requested.
maintenance_and_freshness: A measurement is a pure function of the file, so rerun only for new or changed files (key by the file URL hash, as the font cache already does). Fontsource URLs use @latest, so a Google update shifts numbers slightly; pin the version if reproducibility matters. A new family costs well under a second. The cut-offs are quantiles of the catalog, so look at them again when the catalog grows a lot.
risks_and_limitations: (1) Shape, not mood: Sincere, Innovative, Rugged and Art Deco are not predicted better than category alone. (2) Slant alone is a trap for 'fast': formal scripts dominate its top list; it needs a category or weight filter. (3) One weight and one letter set: a family with several widths or weights is described by the cut I measured. (4) 17 families fail (colour fonts need a browser canvas fallback). (5) Google's tags are per instance in families.csv; anyone keeping the last row per family sees weaker correlations (my first pass did). (6) Validated only on Google fonts; indie fonts have no tags, so transfer is untested. (7) Held-out grouping by first word handles near-duplicate superfamilies only roughly; designers' habits still repeat across families, so AUCs are somewhat optimistic. (8) We learn to agree with Google's labelling, including its noise.
evaluation_hook: Held-out Google tags as I ran it: hide 20% of families (grouped by name stem), predict their tags from traits, report AUC per tag against a category-only model (python3 SCRATCH/vv/analyze2.py, about 1 minute). Plus precision at 20 and 50 for the exact motion query (Active >= 50) before and after the change, and a person rating rendered grids for 20-30 queries with and without the trait words.
recommendation_for_font_explorer: USE IT, and build it first. It is the cheapest, fully deterministic, name-free signal; it covers 99.2% of the catalog including all 339 non-Google rows; and on held-out Google families it beats the category the prompt already has by 12 to 30 AUC points for Active, Loud, Futuristic, Techno and Stiff. Do not expect it to carry mood alone. For 'fonts that imply fast movement or action' use slant on an upright face plus curved outlines and exclude formal scripts (the combination, not slant alone, is what gives the 38-42% hit rate), and let the LLM translate words into traits. Relative to the other items: it is the baseline vision labels have to beat (on the 48-font blind test traits scored AUC 0.94 for Active and 0.99 for Loud against 0.89 and 0.98 for a Sonnet-class model reading images; vision won on Futuristic, 0.89-0.90 against 0.81, and the two combined were best), and it supplies the features for tag transfer to untagged rows. It is also the same-signal alternative to image embeddings for 'looks like' (8-nearest-neighbour same-sub-style share 0.32 from traits alone, 0.36 with category, against 0.28 for category and 0.07 for chance on 1,275 Google families). Smallest first step: port measure.mjs into a server script, write server/data/traits.json, add the trait words to compactCatalog for rows where a trait is extreme (about 7.5k tokens), and run check-vibe on 'fonts that imply fast movement or action' and 'more technological' before and after.
